checks.note: Heading 'Method for solving linear equations' names the topic of the objective. A heading is not required to demonstrate or explain, only to name the topic.

Intro text explicitly states and explains all steps: expand brackets, rearrange variable terms to one side, group like terms, simplify, factor if needed, find solution, and check by substitution. Covers the exact method in the objective.
Worked example demonstrates solving 4(2x-9)-4x=4-6x by: expanding brackets, collecting like terms, rearranging, dividing, and checking by substitution. Exemplifies all objective components.
Exercise equation 6x+3x=4-5(2x-3) requires bracket expansion, like term collection, and solving. Appropriate practice for the objective.

Summary states 'A linear equation has at most one solution' — a property of linear equations. This fact does not address the METHOD (expanding, collecting, rearranging, dividing, checking) required by the objective.
Intro shows the equation example (2-x)/(3x+1)=2 but does not state, define or explain the method. Only introducing the equation type without explanation does not support the objective.
Worked example demonstrates: (1) stating restriction (x≠-1/3), (2) multiplying both sides by denominator, (3) solving, (4) checking by substitution. Exemplifies all objective components.
Exercise equation 2-4/(b+5)=3b/(b+5) has variable in denominator and requires multiplication by denominator and checking. Appropriate practice.
Exercise equation 5-7/b=2(b+4)/b has variable in denominator. Requires solving with variable denominator practice.
Intro shows the equation example (2a-3)/3-3a=a/3 but does not explain the method. Only introducing the equation type without explanation does not support the objective.
Worked example demonstrates: (1) multiplying by common denominator (3), (2) simplifying, (3) rearranging, (4) dividing, (5) checking by substitution. Exemplifies all objective components.
Exercise equation (x+2)/4-(x-6)/3=1/2 has fractions with numeric denominators. Requires finding common denominator and solving.
Exercise equation 2+(a-4)/2-a/3=7 has fractions with numeric denominators. Requires finding common denominator and solving.

reconciled.notes: All seven keys (A1-A3, B1-B4) are placed. A1 and B2 are the same solving objective, and A3 and B3 are the same compound objective. A2 covers both B1 (read an inequality from a number line) and B4 (solve over a stated number set and show it on a number line). Both finders cite the same Ex4-6:1 and Ex4-6:4 items for that material, so I merged them into one objective. A1's wording is used for the solving objective because it separates solving from representing. B2 folds the number-line and interval-notation representation into its solving statement, and A2 owns that part. Objectives are ordered by first printed page: the solving heading (p96), interval notation and the number line (p97), then the compound inequality (WE19, p99). End-of-chapter anchors (Ex4-7:9a and Ex4-7:12p) appear as evidence only. All 29 exercise items and all 3 worked examples are placed once each.
